source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: On a random 100-task ARC subset GPT-4 solves more when it writes natural-language hypotheses first, then Python programs checked on the examples.
numbers: Direct output prediction 17%; program only 23%; summarized hypotheses 30%; human-selected hypotheses 33%; human-written (LARC) hypotheses 45%. Icecuber DSL search (no LLM) 43% on the same items. Setup: 64 hypotheses, summarized to 8, 8 programs each, 3 rounds of execution feedback.
limits: Top-1 accuracy, GPT-4 on text grids, one paper. Direct baseline is weak on ARC.
agent_relevance: S3 GENERATE: propose hypotheses in words, then compile to code. S2 REPRESENT: the program is the representation and is checked by running it.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search, bottleneck analysis
finding: The bottleneck is hypothesis generation, not coding: GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 of 100 ARC tasks.
numbers: Of the 49 tasks with a correct hypothesis, 33 (67%) ended with a correct program. Of 30 tasks solved with summarized hypotheses, 28 had a correct hypothesis before summarizing.
limits: Correct-hypothesis status judged by human annotators.
agent_relevance: Compress many candidate ideas to a few before the costly implement step; the generate step is where help is needed.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search, other datasets
finding: The pipeline helps on easier induction sets, but the language step only matters when the concept is hard to state directly in code.
numbers: 1D-ARC (108 tasks): direct 39.6%, program only 61.1%, full 73.1%. List Functions (100 tasks): direct 31%, program only 59%, full 69%. SyGuS (89 tasks): CrossBeam DSL search 74.8%, GPT-4 program only 94.3%, full 94.3% (3 of 5 failures had mistakes in the examples).
limits: On SyGuS the language hypothesis added nothing. Parsel combinatorial search helped human hypotheses (47.5%) but hurt LLM hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Do not force a hypothesis-in-words step on tasks the model can code directly; gate it by difficulty.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search, Bayesian framing
finding: The authors frame the method as importance sampling in a Bayesian program-induction model (Goodman et al. 2008): the LLM is the proposal, execution on examples is the likelihood.
numbers: Just writing code instead of grids already lifts accuracy: ARC 17 to 23; 1D-ARC 39.6 to 61.1; List Functions 31 to 59.
limits: Authors' own framing; no direct test against a human-fitted prior.
agent_relevance: Most of the lift on structured tasks comes from code-as-representation plus execution checks.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: iterative hypothesis refinement
finding: Propose rules, test them with a symbolic interpreter, refine from failures. This beats input-output prompting, self-consistency and self-refine on 3 of 4 datasets.
numbers: Task accuracy IO vs best refinement (T=3, N=5): ACRE 28.0 vs 59.0; MiniSCAN 0.0 vs 70.0; List Functions 39.6 vs 52.4; MiniARC 13.8 vs 14.6. Self-consistency N=5: ACRE 29.0, MiniARC 13.1. Self-refine with the LM as its own interpreter: ACRE 32.0, MiniSCAN 0.0.
limits: MiniARC raw accuracy: IO 33.1 beat refinement 18.7. Symbolic interpreter feedback is what moves results; majority vote and LM-as-interpreter do not.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G3: revise from real execution output; do not let the model grade its own rule.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: rule application gap
finding: LMs cannot reliably apply the rules they themselves induced.
numbers: Task accuracy with symbolic vs LM interpreter: MiniSCAN about 85-93 vs 0.0; MiniARC 14.6 vs 5.4. Text: drops 'from more than 80% to almost-zero in MiniSCAN'.
limits: Chain-of-thought and self-consistency did not close the gap (Appendix B.3). Raw vs task accuracy mismatch shows IO prompting often answers right without the intended computation.
agent_relevance: Run the hypothesis as code, not by asking the model to simulate it. A written rule is not an executed rule.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: robustness
finding: Rule induction by LMs is brittle to noisy examples and unfamiliar symbols, unlike humans.
numbers: List Functions with 8 exemplars: perturbing 12.5, 25, 50% of outputs lowers accuracy steadily; one noisy example already hurts. MiniSCAN with pseudoword outputs scores lower than English outputs; telling the model about noise helps but the gap stays. OOD longer lists: IO prompting drops more than rule prompting.
limits: Human comparisons only partial (footnote 10: human studies did not cover all experiments).
agent_relevance: Allow a noise tolerance (k misfit examples) instead of requiring a perfect fit; keep a held-out check.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: overfitting to exemplars
finding: Choosing hypotheses only by fit to the given examples can pick rules that do not generalise.
numbers: On MiniSCAN T=3, N=1 beat T=3, N=5; authors blame overfitting because scoring uses accuracy on exemplars only.
limits: Single observation, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Supports G3: a pass on the given examples is not proof; hold out an example.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like Few-Shot Learning via Bayesian Reasoning over Natural Language
finding: An LLM proposes natural-language hypotheses; a prior and likelihood re-weigh them; the prior can be fitted to human ratings. English hypotheses fit humans better than Python ones.
numbers: Number Game: 50-100 sampled hypotheses fit the mean of 8 humans, R2=0.95 (tuned prior); Python code prior fit significantly worse; no-proposal ablation poor; GPT-4 alone differs from humans. Logical concepts (112 concepts, 1,596 humans): R2=0.81 with 100 proposals per batch, within 3% of human accuracy.
limits: Number data average only 8 humans. Computational-level fit, not a process claim. Tuning the prior mattered more for complex logical concepts.
agent_relevance: S3: sample about 50-100 candidate concepts in words conditioned on the data, weigh them by prior and fit in code.

source: Ellis (2023) held-out prediction of new concepts
finding: The model predicted learning speed for two new concepts tested on 16 new participants.
numbers: Majority-colour: model predicts learned after 2 batches, humans fast. Minority-colour: model predicts 4 batches, humans needed 3.
limits: Small N (16), only two concepts.
agent_relevance: Verbal hypotheses let us see which wrong concept a learner may have inferred.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder: wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Wake-sleep program learning grows a library of reusable functions and trains a neural search guide; it rediscovers list functions, vector algebra and physics laws.
numbers: List processing: 218 tasks, 50/50 split, about 20 new routines (filter, then max, then nth largest, then sort). Text editing: 3.7% solved before learning, 79.6% after (40 s average); CVC4 82.4%; DreamCoder with 1 h and 8 CPUs 84.3%. Physics: 93% of 60 laws after 8 cycles. LOGO and towers: nearly 100% held-out vs no baseline above 60%.
limits: Training about a day on 20-100 CPUs. Hand-set starting primitives; no natural-language knowledge.
agent_relevance: S2 REPRESENT: compress repeated solution patterns into named reusable abstractions (a concept library).

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code
finding: LLM synthesis plus Stitch compression plus AutoDoc builds readable concept libraries and beats DreamCoder.
numbers: Online vs DreamCoder: +33.14 REGEX, +20.42 LOGO, +2.26 CLEVR. LLM Solver alone vs DreamCoder: +32.20 REGEX, -5.83 CLEVR, +3.60 LOGO. Offline with learned library vs base DSL: LILO +42.27 REGEX, +63.43 CLEVR, +43.24 LOGO. One LLM synthesis round costs about as much as 48 CPU-hours of DreamCoder search.
limits: Enumerative search still helps on LOGO shapes hard to infer from words. Codex for search, gpt-3.5-turbo for AutoDoc; three domains.
agent_relevance: A library of named helpers with plain-language docs is a usable scaffold object for S2.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO, AutoDoc ablation
finding: Giving an LLM compressed but unnamed abstractions hurt it; naming and documenting them fixed that.
numbers: Stitch compression without docs changed solve rate vs LLM Solver by -30.60 (REGEX), -2.91 (CLEVR), -11.11 (LOGO). Adding AutoDoc: +9.73 REGEX, +2.27 CLEVR, +0.00 LOGO.
limits: LOGO gains absent because of semantic errors in abstractions.
agent_relevance: If the agent keeps learned helpers, store a plain description with each; anonymous helpers can make the model worse.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Two models trained on the same ARC data, one writing programs (induction), one predicting grids (transduction), solve mostly different tasks; the split is stable across seeds.
numbers: BARC ensemble 56.75% on ARC validation (2 tries) vs average human 60.2%, best human 97.8%. Test-time training raises transduction a lot; best published later 61.9% (Akyurek et al. using these models). Ensemble rule: induction first, transduction if no program fits the examples.
limits: Training data are synthetic programs written by GPT-4 and GPT-4o-mini (ARC-Heavy 200k problems). Table text extraction partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Use program induction when the answer is checkable and exact; fall back to a direct answer when no hypothesis fits all examples.

source: Li et al. (2024) induction vs transduction, task types and data quality
finding: Induction wins at precise computation and composing concepts; transduction wins on fuzzy perceptual concepts. Induction is more sensitive to training-data quality.
numbers: Small-model comparison with GPT-4o-mini data: ensemble 26.50%, induction (2048 samples) 18.78%, transduction (beam 20) 15.25%; second data source: ensemble 19.50%, induction 11.07%, transduction 13.50%.
limits: Trained neural models, not prompting.
agent_relevance: Route by task type with a code-checked signal; do not let the model choose its own mode.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC Prize 2024 Technical Report
finding: LLM-guided program synthesis reached 42% on the public ARC set, and every top LLM transduction system used test-time training.
numbers: Greenblatt, GPT-4o sampling thousands of Python programs per task plus debugging: 42%. ARChitects 53.5% private; MindsAI 55.5% (not eligible). Icecuber brute-force DSL search 20% private (2020), 49% for an ensemble of 2020 entries. No static-inference transduction above 11%. Estimate: 85% would need about 100 million programs per task, a multi-million-dollar budget. Humans: two testers 97% and 98%.
limits: Deep-learning-guided synthesis does not yet decisively beat DSL brute force; both near 40%. Scores depend on compute.
agent_relevance: Program induction at scale is a compute trade; keep the sample budget explicit.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC Prize 2024, commercial LLM baselines
finding: Single-pass frontier LLMs without program search score low on ARC.
numbers: Public / semi-private pass@1: o1-preview 18% / 21%; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14% / 21%; Gemini 1.5 5% / 9%; Berman 53.6% / 58.5%; Greenblatt 43% / 42%.
limits: pass@1 API results with frozen prompts; table rows partly ambiguous in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Direct answers are far below search over programs on abstract induction.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini and Moskvichev (2023) Comparing Humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on Abstraction and Reasoning Tasks
finding: On ConceptARC (480 tasks, 16 concept groups) text GPT-4 stays far below humans even with a detailed one-shot prompt.
numbers: Earlier work: humans 91%, Kaggle first-place program 52%, GPT-4 25%. Per concept humans 0.83-0.97, GPT-4 0.13-0.63 (Count 0.86 vs 0.13; Order 0.95 vs 0.60). Minimal tasks (48): humans 0.95, GPT-4 0.69 (temp 0) and 0.65 (temp 0.5), GPT-4V 0.25 zero-shot and 0.23 one-shot.
limits: Single 2023 model (gpt-4-0613); newer models likely higher. Image input did not help on the simplest tasks.
agent_relevance: LLMs fail even simple core-concept abstraction in one pass; checking hypotheses by code is needed.

source: Rule et al. (2024) Symbolic metaprogram search improves learning efficiency and explains rule learning in humans
finding: Searching over metaprograms (programs that revise programs) fits human list-function learning with orders of magnitude less search than plain program search.
numbers: Human data: 392 participants, 100 list functions, about 16 per function. 54% of functions acquired by half of learners within 8 trials; mean accuracy 0.521 (95% CI 0.479-0.559), range 0.042-0.868; 58% of those reporting had no programming experience (mean accuracy 0.49). MPL at 5K steps reaches 84% of its 500K acquisition rate; Fleet falls sharply. 82.8% of metaprograms are at least as simple as their programs.
limits: MPL closer to human accuracy than Fleet at 5K: Wilcoxon V=874, p<0.001, effect 0.39. Recursive problems solved with recursive programs in only 34.4% of MPL runs vs 97.0% non-recursive. Median human response 14.7 s.
agent_relevance: Search over edit operations on candidate programs instead of from scratch: matches revision from a failing output.

source: Rule et al. (2024) Nature Comms, Codex baseline
finding: Codex asked for one Python function per trial acquired about as many list functions as 25th-percentile humans, below the best symbolic search models.
numbers: Few-shot prompt with four example tasks (five pairs each), temperature 0, 150 max tokens. Performance was similar with newly generated pairs, so not simple memorising of public stimuli.
limits: Old model (Codex); no modern-LLM rerun in the paper. Enumerate and Metagol failed on most functions even with tens of millions of steps.
agent_relevance: A one-shot LLM is a weak concept learner; search plus checking is where the gains come from.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Large Language Models can Learn Rules (Hypotheses-to-Theories)
finding: The LLM generates and verifies rules on training examples; rules that appear and help often enough form a rule library used in later prompts.
numbers: Gains of 10-30% over CoT and least-to-most. CLUTRR: +11.1 to +16.4 points average for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; with GPT-4 rules, GPT-3.5 CoT +27.2 points (doubled). Wrong rules cause 65% and 81% of baseline errors on CLUTRR and base-16 arithmetic.
limits: Supervised EdgeTransformer average 71.8 on CLUTRR; CoT+HtT with GPT-4 is 7.5 below it. Needs 2,000 training examples; library must fit in context. Rules from the symbolic version transfer to text for GPT-4 but not GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Fits S2: keep a small verified rule library, with counts in code deciding which rules stay.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Generating Diverse Hypotheses for Inductive Reasoning (Mixture of Concepts)
finding: Repeated IID sampling gives many duplicate hypotheses. Asking first for a list of K distinct concepts, then a hypothesis per concept, raises diversity and accuracy.
numbers: Average test accuracy over List Functions, MiniARC, MBPP+, Playgol-str: GPT-4o-mini 39.2 to 43.7 (+4.5); Llama-3.1-70B +5.0 average gain; other models +3.3 to +4.1. Unique hypotheses out of 8 rise by +0.37 to +1.00. Temperature above 1.33 gave no extra diversity (top-p) and more degenerate text.
limits: Gains are modest; MiniARC accuracy stays 5-12%.
agent_relevance: Matches G4: samples from one model are not independent. Ask for distinct concepts first and dedupe in code.

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Code
finding: The LM writes code, an interpreter runs what it can, and the LM simulates only the lines the interpreter cannot run.
numbers: BIG-Bench Hard single-task: text-davinci-003 Direct 55, CoT 72, CoC 84 (human raters 68); PaLM 2-S Direct 49, CoT 61, CoC 78. Cross-task: 61 and 47. With GPT-4 CoC 91. Algorithmic tasks near 100%, above best human raters.
limits: Pure Python (no LM fallback) fails almost all non-algorithmic tasks. Cross-task few-shot gain for PaLM 2-S only +2.
agent_relevance: A hybrid: code decides, the model fills fuzzy slots (matches schema section 1).

source: Piantadosi and Jacobs (2016) Four Problems Solved by the Probabilistic Language of Thought
finding: Reviews the probabilistic language of thought: concepts as compositions of primitives, scored by a simplicity prior times fit to data.
numbers: Credits Goodman, Tenenbaum, Feldman and Griffiths (2008) as the first pLOT model of Boolean concept learning, building on Feldman (2000) on logical simplicity.
limits: Review, no new data; written before LLM proposers existed.
agent_relevance: Gives the theory the machine studies implement: short-program prior, likelihood from examples, search.

source: Rule et al. (2024) Nature Comms, human replication and difficulty spread
finding: The human list-function result was replicated in a second sample (Supplementary Note 8) and difficulty varies hugely by function.
numbers: Per-function human mean accuracy from 0.042 to 0.868. 50% of functions acquired by at least one person after a single trial, 75% after two, 99% within eight; only 2% acquired by all participants within eight trials. 106 low-effort participants were excluded.
limits: I read the main text only, not the supplement, so replication size is not recorded. Prolific sample, not representative.
agent_relevance: Concept difficulty is very uneven, so a fixed sample budget per task is wrong; spend more search only after a check fails.
